title: This Sask. woman took some birds to a poultry show. Now avian flu is taking her whole flock
summary: More than 18 million birds in Canada, including more than 1.2 million in Saskatchewan, have been lost due to the highly pathogenic disease since 2021.

image.caption: Christina Meyer with Huey, one of her geese that died from avian flu after she attended the Canadian National Poultry Show. (Christina Meyer/Facebook)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
More than 18 million birds in Canada, including more than 1.2 million in Saskatchewan, have been lost due to the highly pathogenic disease since 2021.
CFIA confirms 11 infected flocks connected to national bird show, up from 3 on weekend
Christina Meyer didn't think her birds would win the show.
Still, she gave the chickens a bath to get ready. One of her geese, Frank, even won a second place ribbon.
But after she got home, three geese died from avian flu. Now she's waiting for the rest of the flock of over 100 birds to die or be culled.
"I feel sick to my stomach day and night, knowing what's going to happen. I haven't been able to really sleep. I haven't eaten well," said Meyer, who lives in the Saskatoon area.
Now she wants to spread awareness about the disease.
One of Christina Meyer's chickens taking a bath to prepare for the Canadian National Poultry Show on Nov. 7. (Our latest hobby farm/Facebook)
"I knew that if you have it, it's everybody. What I didn't know was how drastic and quickly it can hit," she said.
Meyer attended the Canadian National Poultry Show held on Nov. 7 in Moose Jaw through the Saskatchewan Poultry Association, which was the site of an avian flu outbreak.
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) has confirmed 11 cases of highly pathogenic avian flu connected to the show, up from three on Saturday.

items: Avian flu outbreak at national poultry show spreads to other provinces: CFIA

blocks.text: This includes five in Saskatchewan, four in Alberta and two in Manitoba, all in non-commercial flocks.
In Saskatchewan there have been two other recent detections in non-commercial flocks not related to the show, according to the CFIA.

blocks.text: Meyer said some breeders have lost years of progress.
"Because it's nationals, it has a bigger draw of people from further away bringing their best birds…. all those genetics and all those bloodlines are gone," she said.
The impact has also been emotional.
"Huey was one that died. He was really special too. He would give me hugs, kind of. He would eat grass out of my hand," she said.
Avian flu ongoing risk, says expert
Stephanie Smith, Saskatchewan's chief veterinary officer, said this is the first time she's heard of avian flu outbreak at a bird show.
"The fact that this was a show where people came from across provinces increases that concern, just because now we have potentially moved the virus many directions," Smith said.
Breeders can decide the risk level they want to take with their birds, and some steps could make shows safer, such as not holding them in the fall or spring, when transmission is higher, she said.
The general approach is to cull flocks in which there have been infections, Smith said.
Birds exposed to avian flu at national poultry show

"At this point if it's in a domestic flock the approach is to cull anything on site that could have been exposed, to try and keep that virus contained and then get it out of the environment as quickly as possible so we're not causing further spread."
Smith said properly cooking poultry and eggs ensures they're still safe to eat.
More than 18 million birds in Canada, including more than 1.2 million in Saskatchewan, have been lost due to highly pathogenic avian flu since 2021.
A notice issued by the federal government says the risk of avian influenza infection to most people in Canada "remains low."
